facts.fact: Valimail research, as cited by the page, suggests sender reputation is behind up to 80% of all email deliverability problems.
facts.quote: suggests is behind up to **80%** of all deliverability problems

facts.fact: The page states that over 70% of small businesses do not have proper email authentication (SPF, DKIM, DMARC) in place, though it gives no source for this figure.
facts.quote: over **70%** of small businesses don't have proper email authentication in place

facts.fact: The page says that, as of recent updates, Google and Yahoo require SPF, DKIM, and DMARC authentication from bulk senders.
facts.quote: As of recent updates, major providers like Google and Yahoo demand it from bulk senders.

facts.fact: The page defines SPF (Sender Policy Framework) as a public list of the servers and tools authorized to send email from a domain, and an email from an unlisted server fails the check.
facts.quote: Your SPF record is a public list of all the servers and tools (like your email provider) that are authorized to send email from your domain.

facts.fact: The page advises pruning subscribers who have not opened an email in six months, calling them dead weight that should be removed after a failed re-engagement campaign.
facts.quote: If someone hasn't opened one of your emails in six months, they're dead weight.

facts.fact: As an illustrative example, the page says that jumping from 1,000 emails a month to 100,000 overnight would trigger provider alarms because providers value consistent sending volume.
facts.quote: If you suddenly go from sending 1,000 emails a month to 100,000 overnight, you’ll set off every alarm bell.

facts.fact: The page recommends double opt-in, where a new subscriber must click a confirmation link before being added to the list.
facts.quote: Implement Double Opt-In: When someone subscribes, send a confirmation email with a link they must click.

facts.fact: The page states that purchased email lists contain spam traps, outdated addresses, and people who will mark the sender as spam.
facts.quote: Purchased lists are riddled with spam traps, outdated addresses, and people who will mark you as spam in a heartbeat.

facts.fact: The page says mailbox providers such as Gmail, Outlook, and Yahoo assign a dynamic reputation score to each sending domain.
facts.quote: Mailbox providers like Gmail, Outlook, and Yahoo assign a dynamic score to your sending domain.

facts.fact: The page lists subject lines beginning with "Re:" or "Fwd:" to fake a personal connection as a deceptive tactic that can send an email to the spam folder.
facts.quote: Nothing screams "spam" faster than starting a subject line with "Re:" or "Fwd:" to fake a personal connection.

facts.fact: The page names "Free," "$$$," "Act Now," "Limited Time," and "Guaranteed" as common spam-trigger words that filters flag, especially when stuffed into subject lines or used in all caps.
facts.quote: Words like "Free," "$$$," "Act Now," "Limited Time," and "Guaranteed" are classic triggers.

facts.fact: The page recommends aiming for at least 60% text and 40% images in an email as a rule of thumb.
facts.quote: A good rule of thumb is to aim for at least **60%** text to **40%** images.

facts.fact: The page states that Validity's Sender Score ranges from 0 to 100, and that a score above 90 is great.
facts.quote: It gives you a score from 0 to 100. Anything above **90** is great.

facts.fact: The page advises paying close attention to a Validity Sender Score that dips below 80.
facts.quote: If you're dipping below **80**, it's time to pay close attention.

facts.fact: The page says fixing a bad sender reputation can take anywhere from a few weeks to several months, depending on the damage.
facts.value: a few weeks to several months
facts.quote: it can take anywhere from a few weeks to several months based on how much damage was done.

facts.fact: The page says a valid DMARC record is a great start even if the policy is set to p=none.
facts.quote: For DMARC, just having a valid record is a great start, even if the policy is set to p=none.

facts.fact: The page recommends checking sender reputation roughly once a week.
facts.quote: maybe a quick check once a week

facts.fact: According to the Adwave article, spam traps are email addresses set up by anti-spam organizations to catch senders who buy lists, and hitting just one can damage a sender's reputation.
facts.quote: These are pristine-looking email addresses set up by anti-spam organizations specifically to catch senders who buy lists.

facts.fact: According to the Adwave article, invalid addresses in purchased lists cause high bounce rates, which signal to mailbox providers that the sender is risky.
facts.quote: These cause high bounce rates, which immediately signal to mailbox providers that you're a risky sender.
